ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in Figure 9, D is a diode, and AB is a parallel-plate capacitor. Between the two plates of the capacitor there is a charged particle P in a stationary state. At the instant when the distance between the two plates A and B is increased somewhat (the two plates are still parallel), how will the charged particle P move?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the figure is a power supply; the upper end is connected by a wire to node a; after node a is connected a diode D, and the direction of the diode symbol shows that it can conduct from left to right, with node b on the right side. Node b is then connected to the upper plate A of the parallel-plate capacitor; the lower plate B of the capacitor is connected back to the other end of the power supply through the lower wire. The charged particle P is located between the two parallel plates A and B. Reasoning: After the capacitor was originally charged through the diode, particle P is stationary, indicating that the electric field force it receives balances gravity. When the distance between plates A and B increases, the parallel-plate capacitance C=εS/d decreases. If the amount of charge Q remains unchanged, then the voltage U=Q/C will increase, causing the potential of point b connected to the upper plate A to tend to rise relative to the power-supply terminal a, thereby putting the diode in a reverse cutoff state, and the capacitor cannot discharge through the power supply. Therefore the amount of charge Q on the two plates remains unchanged. The electric field strength between the parallel plates E=Q/(εS) is determined only by the surface charge density on the plates and has nothing to do with the plate spacing d, so after the plate spacing increases, the electric field strength remains unchanged. Thus the electric field force on particle P remains unchanged and still balances gravity.
